clue.text: Marx brother cut short one known for grumbling

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the name's final letter is dropped

parts.note: Groucho was the moustached, cigar-chomping Marx brother

explanation.surface: A Marx brother whose career was curtailed becomes remembered mainly as a moaner.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouch is a habitual complainer, someone always in a bad temper and grumbling.

clue.text: Well done, like a healthy steak?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a phrase of congratulation
second meaning: food that is beneficial to eat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well done' looks like a steak order, which the second half plays on; it is really praise.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both an exclamation of approval and a description of something wholesome to eat.

clue.text: Veteran's empty bottle?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who served long in the army
second meaning: slang for a drained bottle, a dead man

explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is'. An emptied bottle has 'served its turn', hence the slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means an experienced old hand, and is also old slang for an empty wine or spirit bottle.

clue.text: Form C girl

parts.note: taken as written
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl in a form labelled C.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a form is a year group or class of pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: A form is a school year group or teaching group of pupils, a British school term.

clue.text: Peculiar to clans with bit of deference for their country?

indicators.note: peculiar means odd or strange, so the following words are set in an odd new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just a small piece of it, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of deference

explanation.surface: Something special to Highland clans, done out of respect for their homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peculiar to' reads as 'belonging only to', but 'peculiar' is the anagram signal and 'to' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The clans are the family groups of the Highlands, so the nation they belong to is their homeland.

clue.text: Annoyed over department giving a representative sample

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above, so the first piece sits on top

parts.note: cross means annoyed
a section is a department of an organisation

explanation.surface: An irritated manager hands over a typical sample of a department's work.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-section is a selection typical of the whole, like a slice showing every layer.

clue.text: She first appeared on one in 1887

definitions.text: She first appeared on one in 1887

parts.words: She first appeared on one in 1887
parts.note: surface reading: a woman's debut on some stage in 1887; setter's reading: She is H. Rider Haggard's novel, published in 1887, its name printed on the opening page of the book

explanation.walkthrough: 'She' looks like a person, but it is the title of Haggard's adventure novel, first published in book form in 1887.
explanation.definitionFit: A book's name is first displayed on the page at the front that gives its name and author.

clue.text: Primate with cross and crown

parts.note: an ape is a primate
X is a cross

explanation.surface: A monkey with a crucifix and a crown, like a heraldic emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: The crown of something is its top point, its summit or peak.

clue.text: Splash of colour in opening in dense wood

indicators.note: an opening is a beginning, so only the first letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the first letter of dense
ash is a type of tree and its timber

explanation.surface: A burst of colour seen in a gap in thick woodland.
explanation.definitionFit: A dash of colour is a small amount of it added for effect, a touch or splash.

clue.text: Disturbing experience in river in old Kent town

indicators.note: the first in places the river's letter inside the pair of words that follow

parts.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
R is the map abbreviation for river
Deal is a seaside town on the Kent coast

explanation.surface: Someone had an unpleasant time in a river near an old town in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England; Deal is one of its coastal towns.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful or trying experience that has to be endured.

clue.text: Of little use in Merseyside town Sunday School

parts.note: Bootle is a town just north of Liverpool, in Merseyside
S for Sunday and S for School

explanation.surface: A Sunday School in a Liverpool suburb is judged rather ineffective.
explanation.walkthrough: Merseyside is the county around Liverpool in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootless is an old word for unavailing or fruitless, from boot meaning profit or advantage.

clue.text: Con's portrait — somehow it may make you laugh

indicators.note: somehow means in some unexplained way, so the letters are rearranged by unspecified means

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A convict's portrait, for some reason, is funny.
explanation.definitionFit: A comic strip is a series of drawn frames telling a short joke, made to amuse readers.

clue.text: Fellow less poorly, treated after eating a poisonous plant

indicators.note: after tells us the treated letters come behind the first piece

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so the single letter goes within the other words
treated means worked on or processed, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man feels less ill after treatment, having eaten a poisonous plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' at the end is both the eaten letter and the start of the definition's phrase in the surface; the definition is 'poisonous plant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fool's parsley is a toxic umbellifer resembling true parsley, a weed of gardens and fields.

clue.text: Kitchen utensils — first of them worried pensioner

indicators.note: the first of a word is its initial letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the first letter of them

indicators.note: worried means agitated or shaken up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly person is bothered by kitchen gadgets, the first of them especially.
explanation.definitionFit: These are hand tools for cutting the lids off cans, standard kitchen gadgets.

clue.text: Agree to write

definitions.meaning: first meaning: match or be consistent with
second meaning: exchange letters with someone

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as consenting to send a letter; the two verbs are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to match or tally, and to keep up an exchange of letters.

clue.text: The German bent back rush to find lousewort

indicators.note: something bent back faces the other way, so the article is read from right to left

parts.note: der is a German word for the
to rattle along is to move quickly and noisily

explanation.surface: A German doubles back in a hurry to track down a wild flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Red rattle is the common name of marsh lousewort, whose seeds rattle in their dry pods.

clue.text: Can one run broadcast?

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether a single person can manage a whole broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the person who presents a broadcast is the one who runs it on air.
explanation.definitionFit: An announcer is the presenter who introduces programmes and reads news on radio or television.

clue.text: In the morning I work with a friend

parts.note: a.m. marks the morning
taken as written
to go is to work or function, as a machine does

explanation.surface: Someone describes working each morning alongside a mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend, borrowed into casual English for a pal.

clue.text: No place for canoe, adrift

indicators.note: a boat adrift is loose and out of position, so its letters wander out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Warning that the open sea is no place for a canoe drifting loose.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: a vast sea is no place for a small boat, and the boat's letters, set adrift, spell it.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge open sea is far too rough and wide a stretch of water for a small paddled boat.

clue.text: Travelling round performing, ringing man, husband, at sixty-minute intervals?

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so the tour goes round the next two pieces

parts.note: an actor who is performing is on
a tour is travel round a circuit
he is the pronoun for a man
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A touring performer phones her man, her husband, every hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' suggests telephoning, but here it means encircling; 'performing' is the stage sense of being on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening on the hour occurs exactly at each o'clock, once every sixty minutes.

clue.text: A masseur might mix socially

definitions.meaning: literally, a masseur kneads the tops of a client's arms and back
the idiom for mingling with others, especially people of a different class

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is taken literally for the masseur's work and figuratively for socialising.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to associate or mingle with people, literally standing close enough to touch them.

clue.text: Relaxed card game's ending in one

parts.note: loo is an old gambling card game; with the 's it gives its possessive form

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the last letter of one

explanation.surface: A relaxed card game ends with someone holding one card.
explanation.walkthrough: Loo was a popular eighteenth-century card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose describes something slack or not tight, so relaxed in grip or tension.

clue.text: Specimen given by western sailor after bit of surgery

indicators.note: after places the western sailor behind the single letter
a bit of a word is a small piece, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of surgery
W is the abbreviation for western
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor from the west provides a sample after a minor operation.
explanation.definitionFit: A swab is a sample of cells or fluid collected on a pad for testing, a specimen.

clue.text: Large family left in container

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for left inside the word for a receptacle

parts.note: a can is a container
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A big family has been left in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: A clan is an extended family group, especially one of the Scottish kinship groups.

clue.text: Undisciplined eccentric, a non-qualifier invited to compete

parts.note: wild means unruly or uncontrolled
a card is an amusing, eccentric person

explanation.surface: An unruly oddball is let into a tournament without having qualified.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport a wildcard is an entrant given a place at the organisers' discretion rather than by qualification.

clue.text: Box office has critical role promoting a dance

indicators.note: promoting moves something up, so the back half of the part is brought to the front

parts.note: BO is the standard abbreviation for box office
taken as written
surface padding: it describes the part but supplies no letters

explanation.surface: The box office takes pride in a crucial part promoting a dance show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'critical' is surface padding; the second half of the part moves up ahead of its first half.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolero is a lively Spanish dance in triple time, also the title of Ravel's famous piece.

clue.text: Row endless work with drill makes in Carey Street

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the last letter of the word for work is dropped

parts.note: a bank is a row, as of keys or switches
a machine that runs is working
PT, physical training, is drill in the gym

explanation.surface: Odd instructions for putting together a row of something and a work drill.
explanation.walkthrough: Carey Street in London housed the bankruptcy court, so 'in Carey Street' is an old British idiom for being insolvent.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in Carey Street was a London idiom for insolvency, after the street of the bankruptcy court.

clue.text: Poked fun at editor after drinks

indicators.note: after says the editor's letters come behind the drinks

parts.note: cups of tea are drinks
ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Staff ribbed the editor once the round of drinks was over.
explanation.definitionFit: To tease is to make fun of someone playfully, mocking or ribbing them.
